issues: “(formerly called the Bocha River, which is a corruption)” → not in the CBETA passage (no 舊曰博叉河 gloss); omitted
en_revised: From the lapis lazuli horse's mouth on the western side of the pond flows the Vakṣu River (縛芻河), which circles the pond once and enters the northwestern sea.

issues: “with slight modifications” → CBETA reads 微有繒絹 “there is a little silk” (Mizutani follows the reading 微有增損 “slight additions and omissions”; Beal “with few differences”); translated as CBETA, variant noted
en_revised: The kingdom of Agni (阿耆尼國) is over six hundred *li* from east to west and over four hundred *li* from south to north. The kingdom’s capital city is six or seven *li* in circumference. It is backed by mountains on all four sides, and the roads are perilous and easy to defend. Streams flow around it, and water is diverted to irrigate the fields. The soil is suitable for growing non-glutinous millet, broomcorn millet, winter wheat, fragrant jujubes, grapes, pears, crabapples, and various other fruits. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs of the people are simple and honest. Their writing system is modeled on that of India. There is a little silk. Their clothing is made of felt and coarse wool; they cut their hair short and do not wear headcloths. For currency, they use gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins. The king is a native of the country; he is brave but lacks strategy, and he is fond of boasting of his own achievements. The country lacks a strict code of conduct, and the laws are not well-regulated. There are more than ten monasteries with over two thousand monks, who study the Sarvāstivāda (說一切有部) school of the Hīnayāna. Since their scriptural teachings and Vinaya discipline follow those of India, the students study them using the original texts. Their conduct and adherence to the Vinaya are pure, clean, and diligent. However, they consume the three kinds of "pure meat," remaining attached to the gradual teachings.

issues: “the trees are sparse and spreading” → 林樹扶疎 = the trees are luxuriant and spreading (Beal: “give a grateful shade”)
en_revised: Traveling more than four hundred *li* westward from the city of Suyab (素葉城), one arrives at the Thousand Springs (千泉). The Thousand Springs is an area over two hundred *li* square, with the Snow Mountains (雪山) to the south and level land on the other three sides. The soil and water are fertile and moist, and the trees are luxuriant and spreading; in the month of late spring, the various flowers are like brocade. There are a thousand springs and ponds, which is how it earned its name. The Khan of the Turks (突厥可汗) comes here every year to escape the summer heat. Within the area are herds of deer, many of which are adorned with bells and rings; they are tame and familiar with people, and do not easily take fright or run away. The Khan cherishes and admires them, and has issued an order to his subordinates that anyone who dares to kill or harm them shall be executed without pardon. Therefore, these herds of deer are able to live out their natural lives.

issues: “northern source of the Onion Mountains” → 葱嶺北原 = the northern plateau of the Pamirs (DM itself so in 01.07.01). Note: this excerpt is the 東臨葉河 sentence of 窣堵利瑟那國 (01.11), not the 西臨葉河 of 赭時國
en_revised: To the east, it borders the Yaxartes River (葉河). The Yaxartes River originates from the northern plateau of the Onion Mountains (葱嶺), flows to the northwest, and is vast, turbid, turbulent, and swift.

issues: “traveling southeast” → 從此東南千餘里 has no 行 (“southeast from here more than a thousand li”)
en_revised: From here, more than one thousand li to the southeast, one reaches the country of Feihan (㤄捍國). The country of Feihan is over four thousand li in circuit and is surrounded by mountains on all four sides. The land is fertile, crops grow in abundance, flowers and fruits are plentiful, and it is suitable for raising sheep and horses. The climate is cold, the people are fierce and brave by nature, their language differs from that of other countries, and their physical appearance is coarse and unattractive. For several decades, there has been no great ruler; the chieftains compete for power and refuse to submit to one another, occupying strategic points along rivers and mountains to demarcate their territories and divide their capitals.

issues: “northern source of the Onion Mountains” → 葱嶺北原 = northern plateau of the Pamirs
en_revised: Traveling westward from here for more than a thousand li, one reaches the country of Sutrūṣṇa (窣堵利瑟那國). The country of Sutrūṣṇa is fourteen or fifteen hundred li in circuit. To the east, it borders the Yaxartes River (葉河). The Yaxartes River originates from the northern plateau of the Onion Mountains (葱嶺), flows toward the northwest, and is vast, turbid, turbulent, and swift. The products of the soil and the customs of the people are the same as those of the country of Chāch (赭時國). It has its own king and is subject to the Turks (突厥).

issues: “great mountains (pravaragiri)” → 大山 has no Sanskrit original; the gloss is invented
en_revised: From here, going northwest, one enters the Great Sandy Desert (大沙磧), where there is absolutely no water or grass. The roads are vast and indistinct, and the boundaries are difficult to discern; one must look toward the great mountains and seek out scattered bones to know the direction and mark the path traveled.

issues: “Following the course of the Vakhsh River (縛芻河) downstream to the north” → 順縛芻河北下流 = going downstream along the north bank of the Oxus (縛芻河 = Vakṣu/Oxus, not the Vakhsh; Mizutani: 縛芻河の北に順って流れを下り; Beal: “as it flows down from the north”, also a misreading)
en_revised: Following the Oxus River (縛芻河) downstream along its northern bank, one arrives at the country of Tirmidh (呾蜜國). The country of Tirmidh is over six hundred *li* from east to west and over four hundred *li* from south to north. The capital city of the country is over twenty *li* in circumference; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north. There are more than ten monasteries and over one thousand monks. Regarding the various *stūpas*—which are what were formerly called *futu* (浮圖), and also called *tūpa* (鍮婆), *tāpa* (塔婆), *sītūpō* (私鍮簸), or *sǒudǒupō* (藪斗波), all of which are corruptions—as well as the venerable images of the Buddha, they possess many miraculous manifestations and are spiritually responsive.

issues: “Vakhsh River (縛芻河)” → 縛芻河 is the Oxus (Vakṣu); the Vakhsh is 鑊沙 (01.26)
en_revised: To the southwest, bordering the Oxus River (縛芻河), one reaches the country of Kuwayāna (鞠和衍那國). The country of Kuwayāna is more than two hundred *li* from east to west and over three hundred *li* from south to north. The capital city of the country is more than ten *li* in circumference. There are three monasteries and more than one hundred monks.

issues: “the son of the Western Turkic Yabghu Qaghan” → 突厥葉護可汗: “Western” not in the text
en_revised: To the southwest of the city is the Nava-saṃghārāma (納縛僧伽藍), which was built by a former king of this country. Among the masters who compose treatises north of the Great Snow Mountains (the Hindukush), only this monastery maintains its excellent traditions without decline. Its Buddha images are polished with famous jewels, and its halls are adorned with rare treasures. For this reason, the rulers of various countries have coveted them and sought to plunder them. This monastery has long possessed a statue of Vaiśravaṇa (毘沙門天), whose spiritual insight is reliable and who provides hidden protection. Recently, the son of the Turkic Yabghu Qaghan (突厥葉護可汗), Si Yabghu Qaghan (肆葉護可汗), mobilized his tribes and led his troops to launch a surprise attack on the monastery, intending to seize its treasures. He camped his army in the fields not far from here. That night, he dreamed that Vaiśravaṇa said to him, "What power do you possess that you dare to destroy this monastery?" He then pierced the Qaghan’s chest and back with a long halberd. The Qaghan awoke in a fright and immediately suffered severe heart pain. He told his subordinates of the ominous sign he had dreamed and sent messengers in haste to invite the monks, intending to offer a confession and apology; however, before he could receive a reply, he had already died.  In the southern Buddha hall within the monastery, there is a Buddha’s bathing pot with a capacity of over one *dou*; it is of variegated colors and dazzling, made of a substance difficult to classify as metal or stone. There is also a Buddha’s tooth, over one inch long and eight or nine *fen* wide; it is yellowish-white in color, and its texture is bright and pure. There is also a Buddha’s broom made of *kāśa* grass, over two feet long and about seven inches in circumference, with a handle adorned with various precious gems. Whenever the six days of fasting arrive, these three objects are displayed for offerings as the monastic and lay communities gather; moved by their utmost sincerity, the objects sometimes emit light. To the north of the monastery is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, plastered with diamond-like mortar and adorned with various precious gems. Inside are relics that occasionally emit a miraculous light. To the southwest of the monastery is a vihāra (精廬) that has stood for many years since its establishment. People from afar gather here, and men of high talent congregate; those who have attained the four fruits (catur-phala) are too numerous to detail. Therefore, when the various arhats were about to enter nirvāṇa, they manifested supernatural powers and became known to the public, which led to the construction of their stūpas; the foundations of these stūpas stand side by side, numbering more than several hundred. Although there are also thousands who attained the holy fruit but did not manifest supernatural powers, no monuments were erected for them. At present, there are over one hundred monks who are diligent day and night, and it is difficult to distinguish the ordinary from the holy among them.

issues: “the country of Udyāna (銳秣陀國)” → 銳秣陀 is a different country (Jumadha?, cf. 01.33; Beal Jui-mo-to), not Udyāna/Uḍḍiyāna; “forty li” → 四十餘里 more than forty li
en_revised: More than fifty *li* to the northwest of the great city, one arrives at the city of Trapuṣa (提謂城); more than forty *li* to the north of that city is the city of Bhallika (波利城). In each of these cities, there is a *stūpa* over three *zhang* in height. In the past, when the Tathāgata had first realized the fruit of Buddhahood, he arose from the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) and was on his way to the Deer Park. At that time, two merchants encountered his majestic radiance and, following the provisions they had for their journey, offered him parched grain and honey. The World-Honored One spoke to them of the blessings of humans and gods, and they were the first to hear of the five precepts and the ten virtues. Having heard his Dharma instruction, they requested something to venerate, and the Tathāgata then bestowed upon them his hair and nails. As the two merchants were about to return to their own country, they asked for the ritual of veneration. The Tathāgata took his *saṃghāṭī* (僧伽胝) and folded it square to place on the ground; next he placed his *uttarāsaṅga* (欝多羅僧), then his *saṃkakṣikā* (僧却崎), then inverted his alms bowl, and stood his *khakkhara* (錫杖) upright. In this sequence, he formed a *stūpa*. The two men accepted his command and each returned to his own city, where they modeled their constructions after the holy design and built them accordingly; these were the very first *stūpas* in the Dharma of Śākyamuni. Seventy *li* to the west of the city is a *stūpa* over two *zhang* in height, which was built in the past during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha. From the great city, one goes southwest into the valleys of the Snow Mountains (雪山阿) to reach the country of Jumadha (銳秣陀國).

issues: “the heavenly spirits manifest auspicious signs or show ominous changes to seek blessings and merit” → the subject of 求福德 is the merchants (Mizutani: 福徳を求めさせる); DM makes the spirits seek merit
en_revised: After traveling more than six hundred li, I left the borders of the country of Tukhāra (都貨邏國) and arrived at the country of Bāmīyāna (梵衍那國). The country of Bāmīyāna is more than two thousand li from east to west and over three hundred li from north to south; it is situated in the midst of the Snow Mountains. The people rely on the mountain valleys and build their settlements according to the terrain. The capital city of the kingdom rests against a cliff and spans a valley, measuring six or seven li in length, with high rocks at its back to the north. There is winter wheat, but few flowers or fruits; it is suitable for animal husbandry, and there are many sheep and horses. The climate is cold and harsh, and the customs are rugged and fierce; the people mostly wear garments of leather and wool, which is appropriate for their environment. Their writing, customs, and use of currency are the same as those of the country of Tukhāra. Their language is slightly different, but their appearance and manners are largely the same. Their sincere faith is especially greater than that of neighboring countries. From the Three Jewels above down to the hundred spirits below, there is none to whom they do not offer their sincerity, exhausting their hearts in reverence. For merchants traveling to and fro, the heavenly spirits manifest auspicious signs or show ominous changes, so that they seek blessings and merit. There are several dozen monasteries and several thousand monks, who follow the Lokottaravāda school (說出世部) of the Lesser Vehicle.

issues: “Great Quinquennial Assembly (pañcavārṣika)” → 無遮大會 = an unrestricted great assembly; “quinquennial” is not in the text
en_revised: In a monastery two or three li east of the city, there is a reclining statue of the Buddha entering nirvana, over a thousand feet long. Whenever the king holds an unrestricted great assembly (無遮大會) here, he gives away everything from his wife and children down to the national treasures; once the state treasury is exhausted, he offers himself as a gift, and his officials and subordinates then pay ransom to the monks to redeem him, considering such practices to be their primary duty.

issues: “Great Quinquennial Assembly (Pañcavārṣika)” → 無遮大會 = unrestricted great assembly; “(Paropamisos)” for 黑嶺 is an identification, not in the text
en_revised: From here, traveling east, one enters the Snow Mountains (Himālaya), crosses the Black Range (黑嶺), and arrives at the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The country of Kāpiśī is over four thousand li in circuit; it has the Snow Mountains at its back to the north and is bordered on three sides by the Black Range. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circuit. The land is suitable for grain and wheat, and produces many fruits and trees; it yields fine horses and saffron. Rare goods from various regions are mostly gathered in this country. The climate is cold and windy; the people’s nature is violent and rough, their speech is vulgar, and their marriage customs are chaotic. Their writing is largely the same as that of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國), though their customs, language, and manners of instruction are quite different. They wear garments of wool and clothing made of leather and felt. For currency, they use gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins, the standards and designs of which differ from those of other countries. The king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is wise and resourceful, brave and fierce by nature, and his might intimidates the neighboring regions, ruling over ten or more countries. He loves and nurtures his subjects and reveres the Triple Gem. Every year, he commissions a silver Buddha image eighteen feet high and holds an unrestricted great assembly (無遮大會) to provide for the poor and destitute and bestow alms upon widowers and widows. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas, with more than six thousand monks, who mostly study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. The stūpas and saṃghārāmas are lofty, spacious, vast, and pure. There are several dozen deva temples and over one thousand followers of heterodox paths; some go naked, some smear themselves with ash, and some wear garlands of skulls as crowns.

issues: “great mountain ridge (Skt. pravaragiri)” → 大山嶺 has no Sanskrit original; the gloss is invented
en_revised: Three or four li to the east of the great city, at the foot of the northern mountain, there is a large monastery with over three hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). According to the records of former times, King Kaniṣka of the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) once extended his prestige to neighboring countries and his influence to distant regions. He mobilized his army to expand his territory as far as the east of the Pamirs (葱嶺), and the vassal states west of the river, fearing his might, sent hostages to him. Having received the hostage princes, King Kaniṣka treated them with special courtesy and provided them with different residences according to the seasons: in winter they stayed in the various states of India, in summer they returned to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國), and in spring and autumn they resided in the country of Gandhāra. Because the hostage princes had residences for these three seasons, a monastery was built for each; this monastery is the one built for their summer residence. Therefore, on the walls of the various buildings, the hostage princes are depicted, their appearance and attire quite similar to those of the Middle Kingdom (China). After they were able to return to their own countries, they kept their former residences in their hearts, and although separated by mountains and rivers, they did not cease their offerings. Thus, the present community of monks, whenever the time comes for the entry into or the conclusion of the summer retreat, holds grand Dharma assemblies to pray for blessings and cultivate merit for the sake of the hostage princes, a practice that has continued without interruption to the present day. Beneath the right foot of the statue of the Great Spirit King, located to the south of the east gate of the monastery’s Buddha hall, there is treasure buried in the ground, hidden there by the hostage princes. The inscription regarding this says: "When the monastery falls into disrepair, take this to restore it." Recently, a frontier king, greedy and fierce, heard that this monastery contained much hidden treasure and drove out the monks. Just as he was about to begin the excavation, the figure of a parrot on the crown of the Divine King vigorously flapped its wings and cried out in alarm, causing the earth to shake; the king and his soldiers fell back in terror and collapsed, and only after a long time could they rise, whereupon they apologized for their offense and returned home. On the northern ridge of the monastery there are several stone chambers, which are the places where the hostage princes practiced meditation. Within them are hidden many miscellaneous treasures, and beside them is an inscription, guarded by a yakṣa. Whenever anyone wished to open them and take the treasures within, this yakṣa would manifest various forms through supernatural power—appearing as a lion, a python, a fierce beast, or a poisonous insect—showing great wrath in these strange forms, so that no one dared to attempt an excavation. On a great mountain ridge two or three li to the west of the stone chambers, there is a statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara; if someone prays with utmost sincerity to see him, the Bodhisattva emerges from the statue in a wondrous physical form to comfort the practitioner.

issues: “assumed control over his life” → 有其部屬，總其統命 = took over his retinue and assumed command over them (統命 = command)
en_revised: Two hundred and more *li* northwest of the royal city, one arrives at the Great Snowy Mountain (Mahāhimavat). On the summit of the mountain is a pool; those who pray for rain or for clear weather have their wishes fulfilled according to their requests. According to ancient records, there was formerly an arhat in the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) who regularly received offerings from the nāga king of this pool. Every day at the midday meal, he would use his supernatural powers to sit upon his rope bed and travel through the void. His attendant, a novice (śrāmaṇera), secretly clung to the underside of the rope bed and hid himself. When the time for the meal arrived, the arhat departed; upon reaching the nāga palace, he discovered the novice. The nāga king then invited them both to stay for the meal. The nāga king served the arhat with heavenly nectar, while he served the novice with human food. Once the arhat had finished his meal, he expounded the essential teachings of the Dharma for the nāga king. The novice, as was his custom, washed the bowls for his master. Finding leftover grains in the bowl and being astonished by their fragrance, he immediately gave rise to an evil vow, resenting his master and feeling anger toward the nāga: "May all the power of my merit manifest now, that I may cut off this nāga’s life and become the king myself." At the moment the novice made this vow, the nāga king already felt a headache. The arhat spoke words of instruction and exhortation, and the nāga king apologized for his faults and blamed himself; however, the novice remained resentful and did not follow the instruction to forgive. Once they had returned to the monastery (saṃghārāma), the novice made a vow with utmost sincerity. Due to the power of his merit, he died that very night and was reborn as a great nāga king. Fierce and impetuous, he came to enter the pool, killed the former nāga king, occupied the nāga palace, took possession of his retinue, and assumed command over them. Because of his former vow, he stirred up violent storms and rain, uprooting trees and intending to destroy the monastery. At that time, King Kaniṣka, feeling puzzled, inquired about the matter, and the arhat explained everything to the king. The king then established a monastery (saṃghārāma) for the nāga at the foot of the Snow Mountains and erected a stupa (stūpa) over one hundred feet high. The nāga, harboring his former resentment, proceeded to stir up wind and rain. The king was intent on universal salvation, while the nāga, fueled by the poison of his anger, committed acts of violence, causing the monastery and the stupa to be destroyed six times and rebuilt seven times. King Kaniṣka, ashamed that his work was not being completed, wished to fill in the nāga’s pool and destroy his dwelling; he immediately mobilized his troops and arrived at the foot of the Snow Mountains. At that time, the nāga king, feeling deep fear, transformed himself into an old brahmin, knocked on the king’s elephant, and remonstrated, saying: "Great King, you have cultivated good roots in the past and planted many superior causes, which has enabled you to become a human king to whom all submit. Why, then, do you contend with a nāga today? A nāga is merely an animal, a base and vile species, yet he possesses great power and cannot be contested by force. Riding the clouds and driving the wind, treading on the void and walking on water—these are things not controlled by human power; how could they be objects of the king’s wrath? If the king now mobilizes the entire nation to fight against a single nāga, then if you win, the king will gain no prestige for subduing a distant foe, and if you lose, the king will suffer the shame of being defeated by an unworthy opponent. For the sake of the king’s own interests, it would be best to withdraw the troops." King Kaniṣka did not follow this advice. The nāga then returned to the pool, and with a sound like rolling thunder, violent winds uprooted trees, sand and stones fell like rain, clouds and fog obscured the light, and the army’s horses were terrified. The king then took refuge in the Triple Gem and prayed for protection, saying, "By virtue of the many blessings I cultivated in past lives, I became a king of men, deterring powerful enemies and ruling over Jambudvīpa; that I am now humiliated by this dragon beast is truly due to my meager merit. May all the power of my merit manifest at this moment." Immediately, great smoke and flames arose from his two shoulders; the dragon retreated, the wind grew still, and the clouds and fog rolled away. The king ordered his army to each carry one stone to fill the dragon pool. The dragon king transformed back into a Brahmin and entreated the king again, saying, "I am the dragon king of that pool; fearing your majesty, I submit to you. May the king have compassion and forgive my past offenses. The king nurtures and protects all living beings; why would you inflict harm upon me alone? If you kill me, both you and I will fall into the evil realms; you will be guilty of taking a life, and I will harbor a heart of resentment and enmity—karmic retribution is clear, and good and evil are manifest." The king then made a clear covenant with the dragon, stating that if there were any further offenses, he would certainly not forgive them. The dragon said, "Because of my evil karma, I have received a body as a dragon. The nature of a dragon is fierce and evil, and I cannot control myself; if a heart of anger arises, I may forget what has been stipulated. Now that the king is establishing a monastery (saṃghārāma), I dare not destroy it. I will send one person to keep watch on the mountain ridge; if black clouds arise, they must strike the ghaṇṭā (gong) urgently. When I hear that sound, my evil heart will cease." The king thereupon renovated the monastery and built a stūpa, and the practice of watching for clouds continues to this day without interruption. According to the records of predecessors, there is more than one *sheng* of the Tathāgata’s bone and flesh relics inside the stūpa, and the miraculous events associated with them are difficult to describe in detail. Once, smoke suddenly rose from within the stūpa, followed shortly by fierce flames. The people of the time thought the stūpa had been reduced to ashes, but after gazing at it for a long while, the fire died down and the smoke vanished. Then, the relics were seen like a banner of white pearls, circling the central pillar and winding upwards to the edge of the clouds before whirling back down.
